paragraphs: This paper studies decisions in which gathering information costs money or effort, while waiting carries its own risk. A decision-maker observes a continuous-time process to predict whether an adverse event will occur. That event can end the decision process, so the decision-maker must choose both when to collect another observation and when to stop and make a prediction.

The authors develop a Bayesian model and show that its optimal policy has a rendezvous structure. After each observation, the decision-maker can compute the optimal time for the next observation. The spacing balances two quantities: how new evidence may shift the current belief, called surprise, and the chance that the adverse event happens before the next observation, called suspense.

The paper also characterizes the states in which continuing or stopping is optimal. These choices depend on both the decision-maker’s beliefs and the current value of the observed process. Consequently, belief alone does not fully describe the decision situation: the surrounding context also affects when information is worth acquiring.
neurips-2016-balancing-suspense-and-surp.tldr: A Bayesian model shows how to schedule costly observations and stop under time pressure by balancing belief changes against the risk of an adverse event.

paragraphs: This paper develops a clustering method for data organized along several dimensions. Its starting point is a nonnegative three-mode tensor, which can be understood as an array with rows, columns, and slices. The task is to group entries along all three modes together, so the resulting clusters reflect relationships across the different dimensions of the data.

The proposed method extends spectral co-clustering through a new random-walk model called the super-spacey random surfer. This walk provides the basis for an algorithm that simultaneously clusters the tensor’s modes. Although the initial description uses three modes, the method generalizes to tensors with any number of modes, extending its scope beyond the square, symmetric tensor settings discussed in earlier work.

The authors report better clustering results than state-of-the-art co-clustering methods on several synthetic datasets with known clusters. They also apply the algorithm to real-world datasets. The synthetic experiments support its ability to recover planted group structure, while the real-data applications demonstrate its use for analyzing higher-order observations.
neurips-2016-general-tensor-spectral-co-.tldr: A new random-walk-based spectral method jointly clusters every mode of nonnegative tensor data and outperforms comparison methods on several synthetic datasets.

paragraphs: The paper asks how to learn movement that remains coherent over a long period from expert demonstrations. In sports, a sequence of actions may serve a distant objective, such as reaching a strategic position. Capturing individual actions is therefore only part of the problem; a learned policy also needs to reflect the longer-term purpose connecting those actions.

The authors identify a difficulty with conventional single-scale approaches: they learn one state-to-action policy, which can struggle with cohesive long-term behavior in high-dimensional settings. They propose a hierarchical policy class, implemented as a neural network, that automatically reasons about both short-term and long-term goals. This gives the model an explicit way to address behavior at more than one timescale.

The evaluation focuses on imitating basketball trajectories. Professional sports analysts judged the generated trajectories significantly more realistic than those from non-hierarchical baselines. This finding supports the value of hierarchical modeling for the demonstrated basketball setting, particularly when realism depends on sustained movement patterns rather than isolated decisions.
neurips-2016-generating-long-term-trajec.tldr: A hierarchical neural policy learns short- and long-term goals from demonstrations, producing basketball trajectories judged more realistic than non-hierarchical alternatives.

paragraphs: This paper proposes a sampling approach for approximating the minimum value of a particular quadratic objective. The objective combines a matrix-based quadratic term, a diagonal quadratic term, and a linear term, with the latter two scaled by the problem dimension. The central question is whether an approximate answer can be obtained without computation growing with that dimension.

The authors give a method whose running time is independent of the dimension n. Their analysis specifies a sample count in terms of an accuracy parameter epsilon and a failure probability delta. With probability 1 minus delta, the estimated minimum differs from the true minimum by at most an amount of order epsilon times n squared.

The error scale is essential to interpreting the constant-time claim: the result concerns an approximate objective value with an additive tolerance that grows as n squared. Numerical experiments provide supporting evidence for both accuracy and runtime. Together, the theoretical and empirical results establish sampling as an approach to this stated quadratic minimization problem.
neurips-2016-minimizing-quadratic-functi.tldr: A sampling algorithm approximates a specified quadratic minimum in time independent of dimension, with a probabilistic additive-error guarantee.

paragraphs: Natural-parameter networks address two concerns about neural networks: overfitting when training data is scarce and limited flexibility in choosing probability distributions for weights and neurons. The authors propose a lightweight Bayesian network family that allows arbitrary distributions from the exponential family to represent these quantities, making distributional choices part of the model design.

The network receives distributions as inputs, transforms them through its layers, and produces distributions intended to match the target outputs. Training uses efficient backpropagation to learn the natural parameters that specify distributions over both weights and neurons. The approach therefore carries distributional representations through the network rather than restricting its internal computations to single-valued activations.

The distributions produced at intermediate layers also provide representations that may be useful for associated tasks, including link prediction. The authors describe these as second-order representations. Experiments on real-world datasets show that the method can achieve state-of-the-art performance. These findings support the proposed combination of flexible probabilistic modeling and neural-network training, without making performance a universal guarantee.
neurips-2016-natural-parameter-networks-.tldr: Natural-parameter networks propagate and learn exponential-family distributions over weights and neurons, providing a lightweight Bayesian neural-network approach.

paragraphs: This paper analyzes what happens when stochastic gradient learning revisits the same training data multiple times and optionally processes examples in mini-batches. Its focus is learning with square loss. The question is how choices about passes, step sizes, and batch sizes affect the quality of the learned solution when only a finite dataset is available.

The main result gives the number of passes a statistical role: under a universal choice of step size, it acts as a regularization parameter. Stopping training early can achieve optimal finite-sample bounds. In this setting, choosing when to stop is therefore a way to control learning behavior, rather than simply a decision about how much computation to spend.

The analysis also shows that mini-batches permit larger step sizes. A single theoretical framework covers both batch and stochastic gradient methods as special cases, linking these training procedures within the same account. The resulting guarantees concern the square-loss setting studied in the paper and explain how early stopping and batching can participate in statistically effective learning.
neurips-2016-optimal-learning-for-multi-.tldr: For square-loss learning, early stopping can achieve optimal finite-sample bounds, while mini-batches allow larger gradient step sizes.

paragraphs: The paper studies the consensus problem in distributed optimization, where participating parts of a system must reach a common solution through communication. It investigates whether Min-Sum, a message-passing protocol, can solve this problem. The authors show that the ordinary version does not converge in the setting they analyze, making modification of the protocol necessary for their approach.

They then consider a modified version called Min-Sum Splitting and prove that it converges to the solution. With an appropriate choice of tuning parameters, it achieves accelerated convergence rates described as subdiffusive. These rates match those obtained by shift-register methods, establishing a theoretical connection in performance between different approaches to accelerated consensus.

The paper also identifies similarities between this acceleration mechanism, lifted Markov-chain techniques, and multistep first-order methods in convex optimization. These connections help place the message-passing result within a wider family of acceleration ideas. The guarantee depends on choosing the parameters properly; the result does not say that every configuration of the modified algorithm achieves the accelerated rate.
neurips-2017-accelerated-consensus-via-m.tldr: Properly tuned Min-Sum Splitting solves distributed consensus with provably accelerated convergence, whereas ordinary Min-Sum fails to converge in the studied setting.

paragraphs: This paper develops a way to learn mass matrices for Bayesian samplers based on discretized, energy-preserving dynamics. Existing adaptive approaches can make those matrices depend on the sampled parameters, introducing complicated dynamics, implicit equations, and costly matrix inversions. The authors seek a simpler way to adapt the matrices while retaining existing sampling dynamics.

Their solution uses a Monte Carlo expectation-maximization framework. The sampling step runs the existing dynamics, and the maximization step learns mass matrices through a new online procedure. They also adapt how many samples the expectation step collects, using estimates of sampling error from the leapfrog dynamics. This addresses both the sampler’s matrix settings and the amount of sampling used during adaptation.

The framework is applied to Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, SGHMC, SGNHT, and a new stochastic sampler based on Nosé-Poincaré dynamics. Experiments cover synthetic and real high-dimensional sampling problems. The authors report accuracy comparable to Riemannian samplers with substantially greater speed, supporting the practical value of separating matrix learning from more complicated parameter-dependent dynamics.
neurips-2017-adaptive-bayesian-sampling-.tldr: A Monte Carlo EM framework learns sampler mass matrices and adapts sample counts, achieving accuracy comparable to Riemannian samplers substantially faster in experiments.

paragraphs: Affine policies are widely used in dynamic optimization because finding a fully adjustable optimal solution is often intractable. Their observed performance can be near-optimal even when worst-case guarantees are poor. This paper investigates that gap for two-stage adjustable robust optimization, including the setting with linear covering constraints and uncertain right-hand sides.

The authors analyze randomly generated problem instances. When constraint coefficients are drawn independently from the same distribution within a broad class, they show that affine policies provide a good approximation with high probability. This gives a theoretical explanation for strong empirical performance under those instance-generation assumptions, beyond what a worst-case bound alone can reveal.

They also construct a contrasting distribution whose coefficients are not independent and identically distributed. Under that model, an unfavorable bound of order square root of m holds with high probability. The two results show why the generative model matters: typical performance can be favorable for broad classes of random inputs, while other random-input models still produce poor approximation behavior.
neurips-2017-beyond-worst-case-a-probabi.tldr: Affine policies have strong probabilistic approximation guarantees under broad independent coefficient models, but their typical performance can worsen under other generative models.

paragraphs: Few-shot learning asks a model to recognize new concepts from very few examples. This paper approaches the problem through information retrieval, motivated by the need to extract as much useful information as possible from limited training data. It focuses on how a training batch can supply many relationships among examples for the model to learn.

Each point in a batch serves as a query, and the remaining points are ranked according to their predicted relevance to that query. The authors formulate a structured prediction objective that optimizes mean Average Precision across these rankings. The objective effectively considers all relative orderings of batch points simultaneously, making ranking structure central to the training procedure.

This formulation connects learning a useful representation with retrieving relevant examples. The authors report strong results on standard few-shot classification benchmarks and show that the method also supports few-shot retrieval. The stated findings suggest that a ranking-oriented training objective can serve both recognizing new categories and finding relevant items when examples of a new concept are scarce.
neurips-2017-few-shot-learning-through-a.tldr: A few-shot learning objective treats every batch example as a retrieval query and jointly optimizes rankings to support classification and retrieval.

paragraphs: Visual question answering requires a model to use both an image and a textual question. The relevant information depends on how these inputs relate: answering the joint task requires directing attention toward useful elements across the modalities. This paper studies an attention mechanism designed to learn those relationships and use them to guide what the model attends to.

The proposed mechanism learns high-order correlations between different data modalities. These correlations provide a basis for selecting relevant elements in the inputs. The authors present the mechanism as generally applicable, with the central idea that relationships across modalities can help determine attention for a task that depends on those modalities together.

The paper demonstrates the approach on visual question answering and reports state-of-the-art performance on the standard VQA dataset. This supplies empirical support for using high-order cross-modal correlations to guide attention in that task. The broader contribution is an attention formulation intended for multiple modalities, while the stated performance evidence specifically comes from the visual question answering evaluation.
neurips-2017-high-order-attention-models.tldr: An attention mechanism learns high-order relationships across modalities and achieves state-of-the-art results on the standard visual question answering dataset.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to work backward through a hidden Markov model’s filtering process. Given a sequence of posterior beliefs about hidden states and the system’s dynamics, the goal is to reconstruct information behind those beliefs. The authors consider recovering the observation sequence, recovering observation likelihoods, and estimating both together.

Their approach exploits the algebraic structure of the HMM filter. This allows them to replace a computationally expensive mixed integer linear program with simple linear algebra operations. They also provide conditions under which the desired quantities can be reconstructed uniquely. Those conditions distinguish cases where the posterior sequence identifies one answer from cases where uniqueness is not established.

The authors extend the approach to a more general setting in which the posterior beliefs themselves are observed with noise. They evaluate the inverse-filtering algorithms on real polysomnographic data used for automatic sleep segmentation. The contribution combines a more direct computational route to reconstruction with an analysis of when reconstruction is identifiable and a treatment of noisy posterior inputs.
neurips-2017-inverse-filtering-for-hidde.tldr: Inverse HMM filtering uses linear algebra to reconstruct observations or observation likelihoods from state posteriors, with conditions for uniqueness and an extension to noisy inputs.

paragraphs: The paper addresses unsupervised domain adaptation: learning a predictor for a target domain that has no labeled examples by using a labeled source domain. Its stated assumption is that a nonlinear transformation relates the two domains’ joint distributions of features and labels. This places both the inputs and their associated prediction targets within the adaptation problem.

The proposed method uses optimal transport to jointly optimize a coupling between domains and the target prediction function. Because target labels are unavailable, the target joint distribution is estimated using features paired with the function’s predictions. Learning the correspondence and learning the predictor are therefore connected parts of the same optimization.

The authors show that their method minimizes a bound on target-domain error and provide an efficient algorithm with a convergence proof. They also demonstrate flexibility across hypothesis classes and loss functions through real-world classification and regression problems. On those evaluations, the method matches or exceeds state-of-the-art results, supporting its use under the proposed joint-distribution adaptation framework.
neurips-2017-joint-distribution-optimal-.tldr: Joint optimal transport learns a target predictor and cross-domain coupling together, assuming a nonlinear relationship between source and target feature-label distributions.

paragraphs: This paper proposes a two-phase procedure for training deep neural networks on difficult, high-dimensional, nonconvex objectives. The first phase uses Bayesian sampling to explore the objective landscape and find broad modes, which the authors call fat modes. The second phase uses stochastic optimization to fine-tune the parameters obtained through that exploration.

The sampling phase combines Langevin dynamics with continuous tempering and stochastic approximation. A designed temperature dynamics automatically adjusts the sampler’s temperature. This provides a mechanism for changing exploration during training, with the aim of avoiding early confinement to poor local minima before the subsequent optimization phase refines the learned parameters.

The authors support the approach with theoretical analysis and experiments across various types of neural networks, reporting substantial improvements. The stated motivation is better generalization through a combination of broad exploration and later fine-tuning. Their findings support the possibility of overcoming early trapping through these strategies, rather than establishing that every nonconvex training run will reach a favorable solution.
neurips-2017-langevin-dynamics-with-cont.tldr: A two-phase training method combines automatically tempered Bayesian sampling with stochastic fine-tuning to improve exploration and generalization.

paragraphs: Co-clustering groups samples and features together, using their relationships to uncover shared structure. A bipartite graph represents these relationships with samples on one side and features on the other. The paper observes that graphs constructed directly from an original data matrix usually lack explicit cluster boundaries, so many existing methods need an additional step to obtain final cluster assignments.

The authors propose learning a new bipartite graph that approximates the original while containing exactly k connected components, where k is the desired number of clusters. The graph’s structure therefore directly encodes the clustering. Once that graph has been learned, its components supply the result without a separate post-processing stage.

This approach makes explicit cluster structure part of the graph-learning objective itself. It retains a connection to the observed sample-feature relationships while organizing them into the required components. The authors present extensive empirical results supporting the method’s effectiveness and robustness. The stated contribution is both a co-clustering model and a more direct route from its learned graph to cluster assignments.
neurips-2017-learning-a-structured-optim.tldr: The method learns a sample-feature graph with exactly k connected components, making co-cluster assignments directly available without post-processing.

paragraphs: This paper studies how a deep network can share useful information across multiple tasks as its features become increasingly task-specific. Sharing can be unhelpful when it transfers unsuitable information, while insufficient sharing can leave useful relationships unused. The authors focus on exploiting task relationships within the parameter tensors of multiple task-specific layers.

Their Multilinear Relationship Networks place tensor normal priors over those parameter tensors in a deep convolutional network. The model jointly learns transferable features and multilinear relationships involving tasks and features. This makes the relationships between tasks part of what the network learns across its task-specific layers, rather than treating transferability as a property of the features alone.

The authors report that this joint treatment can alleviate negative transfer in feature layers and insufficient transfer in the classifier layer. Experiments achieve state-of-the-art results on three multi-task learning datasets. These findings support learning structured relationships across multiple layers as a way to improve task sharing, with the reported performance established on those evaluated datasets.
neurips-2017-learning-multiple-tasks-wit.tldr: Multilinear Relationship Networks learn structured task and feature relationships across task-specific layers to improve transfer in multi-task learning.

paragraphs: This paper investigates architectural choices for lossy image compression using deep networks. It focuses on progressive encoders that represent an image through multiple stages. The aim is to improve how accurately the original content can be reconstructed for a given amount of stored information, using better prediction within the compression architecture.

The first design choice is to predict the original image data from residuals within the progressive architecture. The authors find that this makes learning easier and improves approximation of the original content. The second is to learn inpainting from neighboring image pixels before compression. Predicting content from its surroundings reduces how much information must be stored to obtain a high-quality reconstruction.

Combining these choices in a baseline progressive encoder produces an average file-size reduction of more than 60% at similar quality compared with the original residual encoder. This is an empirical comparison for the tested architecture. It shows how improvements in reconstructive prediction can translate into substantial storage savings within the studied progressive compression approach.
neurips-2017-learning-to-inpaint-for-ima.tldr: Two predictive design choices, including learned inpainting, cut average file size by over 60% at similar quality relative to the tested residual encoder.

paragraphs: The paper asks whether two continuous random vectors, X and Y, are independent once a third vector, Z, is taken into account. Starting from independent samples of their joint distribution, the authors turn this conditional-independence question into a classification problem. This permits powerful classifiers, including boosted trees and deep neural networks, to handle complex distributions.

The key challenge is constructing comparison data from the distribution that preserves how X and Y each relate to Z while making them conditionally independent. The authors propose a nearest-neighbor bootstrap for this purpose. They theoretically show that the generated samples are close to the desired conditional-product distribution in total variation distance.

The analysis also connects classification generalization bounds to errors in conditional-independence testing. It accounts for the generated samples being nearly independent rather than fully independent. Experiments on simulated and real datasets show gains over previous methods, especially for high-dimensional testing. The contribution combines a practical classification-based test with theoretical treatment of the synthetic comparison samples on which it relies.
neurips-2017-model-powered-conditional-i.tldr: A conditional-independence test combines powerful classifiers with a theoretically analyzed nearest-neighbor bootstrap to improve high-dimensional testing.

paragraphs: This paper addresses prediction problems whose outputs contain dependencies and take continuous values. Neural networks can model complicated input-output relationships, while probabilistic graphical models describe relationships among output variables. The authors seek to combine these strengths in a setting where both representing structured continuous uncertainty and efficiently extracting information from it are challenging.

They propose non-parametric structured output networks, a modular architecture with two distinct components. One represents a structured posterior distribution non-parametrically; the other provides a discriminative inference scheme. Although representation and inference are separated in the design, both components can be trained together end to end. This permits their learning to remain coordinated while assigning them different responsibilities.

The experiments examine two capabilities: capturing structured posterior densities and computing complex statistics of those densities. Comparisons include output spaces with different levels of expressiveness and established variational and sampling-based inference algorithms. The stated contribution is a framework for jointly learning structured modeling and inference; the abstract describes these evaluations without asserting a particular numerical advantage or universal performance ranking.
neurips-2017-non-parametric-structured-o.tldr: Non-parametric structured output networks jointly train a continuous structured posterior representation and a separate inference component.

paragraphs: This paper studies collections in which each observation is an entire network. The goal is to group networks that may come from different populations. Whether nodes correspond across networks matters: some datasets identify matching nodes in different networks, while others provide no such alignment. The authors develop approaches for both situations.

When node correspondence is available, they summarize each network through an estimated graphon and use that representation for clustering. When correspondence is absent, they construct a computationally feasible feature vector using traces of powers of the adjacency matrix. This provides a network-level summary for the case in which direct node-to-node matching is unavailable.

The methods are illustrated with simulated and real datasets, and the paper supplies theoretical justification through consistency results. The contribution extends the clustering target from parts of a single network to whole networks in a collection. Its two representation strategies make the presence or absence of node correspondence an explicit part of how that collection is analyzed.
neurips-2017-on-clustering-network-value.tldr: The paper clusters whole networks using graphon estimates when nodes correspond and adjacency-matrix trace features when they do not.

paragraphs: This paper studies how many questions an interactive clustering algorithm must ask an expert to recover the optimum clustering. Each question asks whether two elements belong to the same cluster. The authors derive information-theoretic lower bounds and nearly matching algorithmic upper bounds, focusing on how a noisy similarity matrix changes the required number of queries.

Their model assumes similarity values are independent draws from one distribution for pairs within a cluster and another for pairs across clusters. Under this model, side information reduces query complexity from order n times k to an upper bound proportional to k squared times log n divided by the squared Hellinger divergence between those distributions. The divergence expresses how distinguishable the two kinds of pair are.

The resulting bound is information-theoretically optimal within a logarithmic factor in n. The algorithms are efficient and need no prior knowledge of the cluster count or the two distributions. These results quantify how informative noisy similarities can sharply reduce expert queries under the stated independent-draw model.
neurips-2017-query-complexity-of-cluster.tldr: Under an independent similarity model, noisy pairwise side information sharply reduces the expert queries needed for clustering, with nearly matching theoretical bounds.

paragraphs: This paper develops a fast way to identify image regions that matter to a classifier’s scores. The method applies to differentiable image classifiers. It trains a separate masking model that changes the classifier’s scores by hiding salient parts of an input image, using the effect of those masks to learn where relevant image content lies.

Once trained, the masking model produces a saliency map in a single forward pass and generalizes well to unseen images, according to the authors. This is the basis for the proposed use in real-time systems: producing a new explanation requires running the learned model once. The paper reports sharp, interpretable maps without artifacts on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet.

The authors also propose a saliency metric and evaluate the method on ImageNet object localization, where it outperforms other weakly supervised methods. This provides an additional task-based assessment of the regions identified by the model. The contribution combines efficient saliency generation with empirical evidence about map quality and their usefulness for locating objects.
neurips-2017-real-time-image-saliency-fo.tldr: A learned masking model generates saliency maps for differentiable image classifiers in one forward pass and performs strongly on object localization.

paragraphs: The paper addresses a tension in imitation learning for motor control. Supervised imitation can reproduce demonstrations but suffer cascading errors when its trajectory departs from them. Generative Adversarial Imitation Learning can learn more robust control from fewer demonstrations, yet may concentrate on a narrow subset of behaviors and be harder to train.

The authors begin with a new variational autoencoder over demonstration trajectories that learns semantic policy embeddings. On reaching tasks with a nine-degree-of-freedom Jaco arm, smooth interpolation between these embeddings produces smoothly changing reaching behavior. This demonstrates that the learned policy representation captures variation that can be used to generate intermediate behaviors.

They then use these representations in a modified GAIL approach. The resulting controller is substantially more robust than the purely supervised controller, especially with few demonstrations, and captures diverse behaviors while avoiding the mode collapse observed with GAIL alone. Demonstrations include learning varied gaits for a two-dimensional biped and a 62-degree-of-freedom three-dimensional humanoid in MuJoCo.
neurips-2017-robust-imitation-of-diverse.tldr: Learned policy embeddings combined with adversarial imitation improve controller robustness while preserving diverse demonstrated behaviors.

paragraphs: The paper develops an image recognition architecture inspired by how people direct their visual attention. It uses a saliency map, which represents which image regions stand out, to guide a sequence of observations. Its hierarchy lets the model select a salient region and then take additional glimpses within that region, combining region selection with closer inspection.

The prediction task goes beyond listing the categories present in an image. The model predicts a multiset: a collection that can contain repeated labels. For example, two instances of the same category can contribute two occurrences of that category’s label. This makes repeated objects part of the prediction target.

A reinforcement learning training process allows arbitrary label order and multiple occurrences of each label. That flexibility matters because a collection of objects does not inherently require one fixed ordering, even when the model examines the image sequentially.

On the proposed multiset task, the authors report high precision and recall, alongside object localization through attention. These findings indicate that the architecture can identify the requested labels while directing attention toward object locations, connecting recognition with selective visual inspection.
neurips-2017-saliency-based-sequential-i.tldr: A hierarchical attention model examines salient image regions sequentially and uses reinforcement learning to predict unordered labels that can include repeated object categories.

paragraphs: Gaussian-process predictions depend on the kernel describing relationships between function values. For long-range extrapolation, uncertainty about the kernel’s parameters can strongly affect predictions. This paper models that uncertainty through a distribution over kernels, constructed by placing a Lévy process over a spectral mixture density.

The resulting distribution supports all stationary covariance functions, including RBF, periodic, and Matérn kernels. Its prior favors sparse mixtures, allowing the model to select its complexity automatically and remove unnecessary components. This links flexible kernel learning with spectral regularization: the representation can accommodate varied covariance patterns while discouraging extraneous mixture terms.

The authors exploit the process’s algebraic structure to obtain O(n) training and O(1) prediction costs. Their benchmarks demonstrate long-range extrapolation with reasonable uncertainty estimates, recovery of flexible ground-truth covariances, and robustness to initialization errors. They also report state-of-the-art predictive performance. These findings support the proposed combination of kernel uncertainty, automatic complexity selection, and computational scalability for the evaluated prediction problems.
neurips-2017-scalable-levy-process-prior.tldr: A Lévy-process prior learns flexible stationary kernels with uncertainty and automatic complexity selection, supporting scalable Gaussian-process extrapolation.
